title: Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical classical computer built around superconducting logic that uses substantially less total electrical energy to perform useful work than a comparable CMOS computer. Its advantage would have to survive the energy costs of refrigeration, memory, communication interfaces, power supplies and other supporting equipment. The target is an integrated, memory-rich machine capable of meaningful high-performance or data-center workloads, rather than an exceptionally efficient switching device or a small processor demonstration.

Josephson-junction circuits offer very low switching energies and low-loss superconducting interconnects, but require cryogenic operation. Different logic families exploit these properties differently: single-flux-quantum, or SFQ, logic communicates through quantized voltage pulses, whereas adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron, or AQFP, logic represents and transmits data using positive or negative currents. AQFP provides a demonstrated adiabatic implementation path; describing all superconducting logic as transmitting tiny flux pulses would obscure this distinction.

Installation in an ordinary-temperature data center would still require a cold computing subsystem. It would not mean that the superconducting logic operates at 300 K. The defining achievement would be superior energy efficiency across the complete operating system boundary, while delivering comparable computational results and performance.

significance.text: A demonstrated tenfold reduction in total energy for equivalent useful computation would be a substantial advance in computer engineering. At a fixed amount of work, it would directly reduce operating electricity consumption; within a fixed electrical-energy budget, it could permit more computation. This impact depends on measuring the complete machine rather than extrapolating from the energy of an individual Josephson device. The tenfold magnitude is the proposed impact threshold for this record, not an established scientific standard.

Imec's May 2024 account supplies a concrete basis for considering much larger gains: it projects approximately one hundred times the energy efficiency of the most efficient contemporary supercomputer and describes a compact stack of computing boards. Those are system projections, not demonstrated performance. Their realization could substantially improve computing density, but the shoebox comparison applies to the computing-board stack and does not establish a shoebox-sized installation containing all refrigeration and supporting equipment.

Lower total ownership cost and smaller complete installations are conditional downstream possibilities. They also depend on fabrication cost and yield, packaging, refrigeration hardware, reliability, maintenance and facility infrastructure. Superconducting interconnects and low switching energies provide technical reasons for pursuing these benefits, but neither property guarantees them. Cooling and other overheads can consume the device-level savings; a small measured system advantage would fall short of the revolutionary-impact threshold proposed here even if the chips function successfully.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is an integrated superconducting computer that sustains an energy advantage across useful workloads after all system costs are counted. The engineering challenge is to close the gap between small, low-energy circuits and a complete machine with adequate memory, dependable clock and power distribution, practical interfaces and effective refrigeration. The supplied 2020–2021 processor study and 2024 system account document this integration gap at their respective dates; they do not establish whether it remains unclosed as of November 1, 2026.

Memory must provide sufficient capacity and bandwidth without overwhelming the logic's energy savings or constraining the machine to unusually small problems. Clock and power distribution must support many interacting circuits while preserving reliable operation and a favorable energy budget. The MANA paper describes memory limitations, manual integration and design-automation challenges, showing why a functioning processor does not by itself establish a scalable computing platform.

Packaging and thermal integration must connect cold logic, memory and warmer interfaces without losing the system advantage. Imec's proposed arrangement places superconducting processors near 4 K and conventional DRAM near 77 K, and its roadmap includes three-dimensional superconducting integration and cooling technologies. These are concrete integration requirements, not merely a need for faster logic. The MANA paper likewise estimates a refrigerated large system while leaving physical insertion and interfacing logistics outside that estimate.

current_state.text: Ayala and colleagues demonstrated MANA, a 4-bit AQFP microprocessor operating at 4.2 K, in work reported in a December 28, 2020 university release and published in IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 56, 1152–1165 in 2021. Full-processor demonstrations ran at 100 kHz. The reported programs exercised register-file reads and writes, arithmetic and logic operations, hardware stalling and branching. A separate execution-unit breakout chip operated up to 2.5 GHz. The gigahertz result therefore establishes component capability, not operation of the complete MANA processor at that frequency.

The university release attributes an approximately eightyfold cooling-adjusted efficiency advantage to the AQFP technology. The research notes describe a comparison with a 7 nm FinFET reference, but the supplied review does not establish a complete-system benchmark or sufficiently comparable useful-work conditions for that number. It should therefore remain an attributed technology comparison rather than a measured data-center energy advantage. The paper's hypothetical large-system budget estimates about 2 MW of total power, including refrigeration and non-refrigerated interfaces, supplies and storage; it is a system estimate, not an operating-machine measurement.

In the May 15, 2024 IEEE Spectrum article “How to Put a Data Center in a Shoebox,” Imec authors Anna Herr and Quentin Herr describe calculations in which superconducting computing becomes more power-efficient than conventional computing at roughly 10^16 floating-point operations per second. They model a stack of 100 boards occupying about 20 × 20 × 12 centimeters and project approximately one hundred times the energy efficiency of the most efficient contemporary supercomputer. The shoebox dimensions describe that modeled board stack. They do not establish the volume of a complete cooled installation, and the projected energy advantage is not a measured workload-level wall-plug result.

The supplied evidence thus documents a small processor, faster component circuits and ambitious system models. It does not report a complete useful-scale machine demonstrating the proposed wall-plug advantage, and it contains no substantive progress record after the 2024 account. Whether a qualifying system had been achieved by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved; the absence of such evidence in this record is not proof that no subsequent achievement exists.

The processor findings above rest on the full MANA paper described in the supplied review: the retained IEEE HTML copy was empty, but a complete PDF independently provided the relevant experimental prose. The review did not visually inspect the figures. The Spectrum projections and university-release statements were available as complete article text. These access boundaries support the prose-based distinctions made here while leaving figure-level interpretation outside the supplied assessment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance criterion: a complete cryogenic computer should perform recognized high-performance or data-center workloads using at least ten times less measured wall-plug energy than the best available comparable CMOS system. Comparisons should require equivalent work and output quality, with explicit throughput or completion-time requirements, so that slower execution cannot masquerade as improved efficiency through lower instantaneous power. The tenfold threshold is an editorial proposal for this innovation, not a published consensus or a threshold prescribed by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Tenfold less wall-plug energy than best CMOS on equivalent workloads

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement boundary: include cryocoolers, memory, interfaces, power supplies and all supporting equipment required to execute the workloads, and apply a consistent boundary to the CMOS comparator. Report workload definitions, numerical precision or other output-quality requirements, elapsed time, throughput, total energy and relevant operating conditions. State how cooldown, startup and idle energy are treated and how that treatment relates to the intended deployment. Memory capacity and bandwidth should accommodate the selected workloads without making memory shortages or artificial problem-size restrictions the dominant limit.
completion_criteria.label: Report consistent full-system energy accounting and adequate memory

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: publish sufficiently detailed hardware configurations, benchmark procedures and energy measurements for independent repetition, with measurement uncertainty and repeated runs. Test a meaningful range of workloads, including cases that exercise memory and communication as well as computation, and demonstrate sustained reliable operation. Such finite tests would establish the breadth actually demonstrated; they would not prove an advantage for every possible application. Any advantage confined to particular workloads, utilization levels or installation sizes should be stated explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatable sustained multi-workload results with explicit advantage limits

completion_criteria.text: The existing 4-bit MANA demonstration would not satisfy these proposed criteria because its demonstrated scope does not establish useful-scale workload performance or complete-system energy superiority. Imec's hundredfold estimate remains a projection to test, rather than either a demonstrated result or the acceptance threshold. A practical qualification would require new system measurements beyond the component experiments and modeled budgets described in the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: New system measurements beyond component experiments and modeled budgets

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CPE-02, “Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer,” has the closest conceptual overlap because AQFP supplies an adiabatic route within superconducting classical computing. Adiabatic operation, logical reversibility and operating temperature are distinct properties. Demonstrating a wall-plug-superior superconducting machine near 4 K would not establish a room-temperature reversible processor; demonstrating room-temperature reversible computation would not establish the superconducting system advantage required by CPE-06. The supplied roster establishes CPE-02's identity, but no detailed CPE-02 research record is available here.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-01, “Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer,” and CPE-07, “Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet,” concern quantum computation and quantum communication, respectively. CPE-06 concerns classical computation even when its circuits exploit superconducting quantum phenomena. Cryogenic hardware or related device technology could create engineering overlap, but success in CPE-06 would not demonstrate quantum fault tolerance or a quantum-repeater network.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-03, “General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance,” overlaps through the importance of memory access and communication energy. CPE-06 must control those costs to preserve a system advantage, but an efficient superconducting computer would not automatically show that data movement no longer dominates general-purpose computation. CPE-04, “Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory,” likewise targets an alternative computing platform with demanding memory and interconnect integration; its optical logic and memory requirements remain distinct from superconducting classical logic.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-05, “Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy,” shares the ambition of a major energy-efficiency advance, but its learning architecture, scale and biological comparison differ from CPE-06's useful-work comparison against CMOS. CPE-08, “Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer,” emphasizes density, manufacturability and defect tolerance. Those could affect practical computer economics, but atomic-density fabrication and superconducting wall-plug superiority are separate achievements. These relationships follow from the supplied titles rather than detailed evidence for the other concepts.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish progress after the May 2024 Imec account or whether a qualifying system existed by November 1, 2026.

The approximately eightyfold claim lacks a demonstrated complete-system useful-work comparison in the supplied evidence; the precise basis and comparability of the research notes' 7 nm FinFET reference remain unresolved.
The refrigeration equipment, supporting infrastructure and total installation footprint associated with Imec's modeled shoebox-sized computing stack are not established.
No supplied measurements establish useful-scale memory adequacy, sustained reliability, manufacturing economics or total ownership cost for a system meeting the proposed energy criterion.
Historical item 9 and the historical thousandfold figure cannot be verified from the supplied inputs.

Detailed companion records are absent for the other roster entries. The recommendation to remove the CPE-02 cross-reference was not adopted in full because the supplied roster permits a clearly qualified conceptual comparison; its detailed research overlap remains unverified.
The proposed benchmark suite, comparator-selection procedure and treatment of startup and idle energy would need to be specified for an actual qualification exercise.

brief.title: Computers that do more with less electricity
possible: Data centers could run demanding computing jobs using a tenth of today’s electricity, including the energy needed for cooling and memory. The machine would use superconducting circuits, which carry current without electrical resistance when kept extremely cold.
why: For data-center operators, lower electricity use would mean less energy spent on the same work. With a fixed electricity budget, it would allow more computation.

sources.who: Christopher L. Ayala and colleagues at Yokohama National University
sources.showed: They built MANA, a small superconducting processor that ran programs with arithmetic, memory access and branching. A separate chip containing its processing units reached 2.5 GHz.
sources.quote:
We also successfully demonstrated a high-
speed breakout chip of the microprocessor execution units up to
2.5 GHz.
sources.cited_for: Superconducting circuits can perform both computation and memory operations.
sources.not_established: The processor did not demonstrate useful-scale computing with lower total electricity use than a comparable conventional machine.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.

sources.who: Anna Herr and Quentin Herr at Imec
sources.showed: Their calculations projected a hundredfold energy-efficiency gain over a leading supercomputer. Their design combines cold processors, memory and connections to equipment at room temperature.
sources.quote:
Our research shows that starting at around 10
16
floating-point operations per second (tens of petaflops) the superconducting computer handily becomes more power efficient than its classical cousin.
sources.cited_for: System calculations give a reason to pursue large superconducting computers despite their cooling needs.
sources.not_established: The projected energy savings have not been demonstrated by an operating machine performing comparable useful work.

shown: Ayala’s team demonstrated a small working processor, with faster processing units tested separately. Imec developed a design and calculations for a much larger system. Neither demonstration establishes the total electricity savings of a complete machine doing demanding computing jobs.
missing: A complete machine would have to beat a comparable conventional computer after cooling and all supporting equipment are counted.
Enough memory and fast enough data transfer would have to support demanding jobs without consuming the circuits’ energy savings.
The cold circuits, warmer interfaces and cooling equipment would have to work together reliably during sustained operation.

milestones.label: A complete computer uses tenfold less electricity
milestones.explanation: A complete machine would have to use tenfold less electricity than the best comparable conventional computer on equivalent jobs at comparable speed and quality. This would establish the intended scale of savings.

milestones.label: Energy measurements cover everything, with enough memory
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to include cooling, memory and supporting equipment, with consistent rules for startup and idle energy and enough memory for the jobs. This would make the comparison fair.

milestones.label: Savings persist across repeatable, sustained computing jobs
milestones.explanation: Repeated, independently reproducible tests would have to show reliable savings across jobs that stress computation, memory and communication. This would establish where the advantage holds and where it ends.

milestones.label: A practical machine delivers new measured results
milestones.explanation: New measurements would have to establish useful-scale performance and total energy savings in an operating machine. Small circuit experiments and projected budgets cannot establish that result.

uncertain: The tenfold target is a proposed acceptance threshold, rather than an agreed scientific standard.
Which jobs, comparison machines and rules for startup and idle energy would make a fair test remains to be specified.
The size and cost of a complete cooled installation remain uncertain; a compact stack of computing boards does not settle either question.

page.title: Superconducting classical computing with lower wall-plug energy
page.definition: A superconducting classical computer completes the same workload as a CMOS (complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor) computer in the same or less time, to the same numerical tolerance, using less electricity. Both totals include memory, interfaces, power conversion and cooling. Single-flux-quantum logic transmits voltage pulses whose time integral is one magnetic flux quantum. Adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic encodes a bit in the direction of a current. An 8-bit single-flux-quantum processor has operated at 57.2 GHz and 11.2 mW, measured at the processor.

goal.need: Data centres used about 485 TWh of electricity worldwide in 2025. In conventional processors, moving data between logic and memory consumes power alongside arithmetic. A supercomputing site at its power limit could run more jobs, including model training, if each job used less electricity. Superconducting switches and wires can reduce both costs, but the savings must cover memory, interfaces and refrigeration. One large-system design requires 395 W of electrical input to remove 1 W of heat at 4.4 K.

statements.quote: Can we build a superconducting computer that is capable of solving important problems?
For the first generation, the road map envisions the stacking of about 100 boards to obtain the target performance of 20 exaflops.
statements.context: Anna Herr and Quentin Herr describe a modeled system using BF16, a 16-bit floating-point format, with projected total power of 500 kW.

statements.body: IEEE International Roadmap for Devices and Systems, CEQIP focus team
statements.quote: a necessary first step is to develop small-scale systems and markets.
statements.context: Section 2.2.1.1 discusses superconducting digital computing for high-performance computers and data centres.

completion.title: A superconducting computer uses less total electricity than CMOS on the same validated HPL problem.
completion.criterion: An integrated superconducting computer and an identified contemporary CMOS computer solve the same HPL dense linear system in 64-bit floating-point arithmetic. Report both configurations and the matrix order. Both solutions must pass the HPL scaled-residual check with the threshold set to 16. The superconducting run must finish in equal or less time and use fewer joules. Measure electricity over each full run with both machines at operating temperature, including memory, communication, interfaces, host and control equipment, power conversion and cooling on each side. The result applies to that problem and those configurations.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback. No outside body defines the combined comparison. HPL defines the numerical validation test.
completion.threshold_quote:
A solution is considered numerically correct when this quantity is less than a threshold value of
16.
completion.basis: HPL defines the double-precision problem and scaled residual. The HPC power-measurement methodology provides a precedent for full-run, whole-system measurements. The matched CMOS comparison, elapsed-time condition and strict inequality in total joules are Atlas criteria. C3's notional prototype is one route to an integrated machine.

milestones.title: Superconducting subcircuits deliver 10^9 bit-operations/s and 10^16 bit-operations/J at 4 K.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a superconducting subcircuit with 10⁴ Josephson junctions at a density of 10⁵ junctions/cm², throughput of 10⁹ bit-operations/s and efficiency of 10¹⁶ bit-operations/J at 4 K. The efficiency refers to energy dissipated at the cold stage.
milestones.set_by: IARPA C3 base-period targets for the SFQ logic track, slide 22.

milestones.title: A superconducting processor reaches 10^11 bit-operations/s alongside 1,024-bit cryogenic memory chips.
milestones.criterion: C3 option-period-2 circuit targets: 10^5 junctions, 10^6 junctions/cm², 10^11 bit-operations/s and 10^17 bit-operations/J at 4 K. Main/cache memory targets: 1,024 bits each; densities 10^7/10^6 bits/cm²; burst rates 5/30 Gbit/s; mean access times 5,000/400 ps; mean access energies 10^-16/10^-17 J/bit. AQFP’s MANA demonstration and the imec fabrication result in m1 do not establish this processor-and-memory combination.
milestones.set_by: IARPA C3, slide 22: option-period-2 SFQ targets; thresholds tabulated.

milestones.title: A superconducting computer integrates a 64-bit CPU, two accelerators and 256 MiB of main memory.
milestones.criterion: Integrate one 64-bit CPU, two parallel accelerators and 2²⁸ bytes (256 MiB) of main memory in a superconducting computer. The C3 prototype targets are a 10 GHz logic clock, throughput of 10¹³ bit-operations/s, efficiency of 10¹⁵ bit-operations/J at 4 K and input/output at 10⁹ bit/s. The efficiency is evaluated at the cold stage, before refrigeration power is counted.
milestones.set_by: IARPA C3, slide 21: notional SFQ prototype; thresholds tabulated.

milestones.title: A superconducting 8-bit adder produces correct sums and has its operating power measured.
milestones.criterion: Operate a fabricated superconducting adder on pairs of 8-bit inputs and verify the sum outputs against the expected bits. Measure active circuit dissipation and report the clock frequency and operating temperature for that measurement.
milestones.set_by: Experimental 8-bit adder benchmark used in reciprocal quantum logic and AQFP studies.

RQL 8-bit carry-look-ahead (CLA) adder as a bench-
mark

milestones.title: A 64-bit cryogenic array meets the C3 main-memory or cache targets.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a functional 64-bit cryogenic array and identify its role. For main memory, the targets are 5 × 10⁶ bits/cm², 5 Gbit/s burst rate, 5,000 ps mean access time and 5 × 10⁻¹⁶ J/bit mean access energy. For cache, the corresponding targets are 5 × 10⁵ bits/cm², 30 Gbit/s, 400 ps and 5 × 10⁻¹⁷ J/bit.
milestones.set_by: IARPA C3 option-period-1 cryogenic-memory targets, slide 22.

milestones.set_by: IARPA C3 option-period-1 targets for the SFQ logic track, slide 22.

milestones.title: A cryogenic memory cell stores one bit and meets the C3 targets for main memory or cache.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a functional 1-bit cryogenic cell with a 1 Gbit/s burst rate and identify its role. The main-memory targets are 10⁶ bits/cm², 10,000 ps mean access time and 5 × 10⁻¹⁶ J/bit mean access energy. The cache targets are 10⁵ bits/cm², 1,000 ps and 5 × 10⁻¹⁷ J/bit.

not_found: No externally published acceptance test combining a complete superconducting computer, a matched CMOS workload and measured refrigeration-inclusive energy superiority was found.
No experimental report located through 25 November 2026 demonstrates the combined C3 prototype targets or a matched HPL run using less refrigeration-inclusive electricity than CMOS.
No academy or roadmap committee statement was found concluding that a refrigeration-inclusive energy advantage for classical superconducting computing is unattainable or unworthy of pursuit.

results.quote: A superconductor single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic 8-bit microprocessor is demonstrated up to 57.2 GHz with a measured power consumption of 11.2 mW.

results.finding: One fabricated SFQ string-matching processor demonstrated 32-bit parallel processing at 12 GHz.
results.detail: The source reports clock speed, but does not establish 10^11 bit-operations/s or the specified 1,024-bit cryogenic memory chips and other circuit and memory targets.
results.quote: Our chip has been fabricated and tested, revealing not only its capability for 32-bit bit-parallel processing at a high speed of 12 GHz but also its achievement of an energy efficiency ratio of up to 251 GOPS/W.

results.finding: One AQFP SR-loop memory cell demonstrated 3-bit storage.
results.detail: The cell was tested at 4 K, with experimental testing limited to kHz frequencies. The paper does not demonstrate 1,024-bit memory chips alongside a processor meeting the circuit targets.
results.quote:
The 3-bit SR-Loop memory cell was fabricated in the MITLL
SFQ5ee process [9] and tested at 4 K in a liquid Helium
immersion probe using an Octopux measurement system [10].

results.finding: One AQFP microprocessor prototype, MANA, was demonstrated with a 4-bit word size.
results.detail: The release gives no operating clock for the full processor. It cites a peer-reviewed paper for the prototype demonstration.
results.quote: we did this by developing and successfully demonstrating a prototype 4-bit AQFP microprocessor called MANA (Monolithic Adiabatic iNtegration Architecture), the world's first adiabatic superconductor microprocessor

results.finding: The AQFP execution-stage chip produced correct sums on 7 of 12 chips, with the best sample passing the carry test at 2.5 GHz.
results.detail: The high-speed test toggled only the least significant bit of one operand while holding the other input bits fixed.
results.quote:
For our best sample, we conﬁrmed functional operation at
1, 2, and 2.5 GHz and measured excitation margins of AC1
and AC2 to be 2.6 and 2.4 dB, respectively, at 2.5 GHz,
as seen in Fig. 12.

results.finding: MANA demonstrated access to a 64-bit-organized cryogenic register file in processor tests that succeeded on 5 of 6 chips.
results.detail: The register file occupied 4.7 × 6.6 mm. The reported 100 kHz was the processor clock used in testing.
results.quote:
The RFX stage is a two-read/one-write 16 × 4 b RF with
registers $14 and $15 to hold I/O data, and $0 as a constant
zero register.

results.finding: The fabricated MANA AQFP processor executed test programs at 100 kHz on 5 of 6 chips.
results.detail: The 2.5 GHz result applies to a separate ALU and shifter breakout chip. The 5 GHz value applies to a junction switching-energy result cited from prior work.
results.quote:
We demonstrate
register ﬁle R/W access, ALU execution, hardware stalling, and
program branching performed at 100 kHz under the cryogenic
temperature of 4.2 K.

results.finding: One fabricated 8-bit superconducting adder design produced correct sums and dissipated an estimated 510 nW in its active core.
results.detail: The core estimate uses a correction for phase modulation and allocates a share of measured chip dissipation to the adder core, excluding the input shift register and output amplifiers.
results.quote:
Measured power dissipation of the fully active circuit is only 510 nW at
6.2 GHz.

results.finding: AC-clocked SFQ shift registers with self-shunted junctions reached 7.4 × 10⁶ junctions/cm² (sample size unstated).
results.quote:
Using self-shunted JJs with J

results.finding: One fabricated AQFP 8-bit carry look-ahead adder dissipated an estimated 1.5 aJ per operation.
results.detail: The reported 24k(B)T per junction expresses energy in thermal units without giving a numerical operating temperature.
results.quote: Our results showed that the energy dissipation per operation of the 8-bit CLA can be estimated to be approximately 1.5 aJ, or 24k(B)T per junction, where k(B) is the Boltzmann constant and T is the operating temperature.

results.finding: One 8-bit SFQ microprocessor operated at up to 57.2 GHz.
results.detail: The clock rate and measured power alone cannot establish bit-operation throughput or energy efficiency. The supplied text identifies a conference proceedings contribution and gives no evidence of peer review or independent replication.
results.quote: A superconductor single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic 8-bit microprocessor is demonstrated up to 57.2 GHz with a measured power consumption of 11.2 mW.

results.finding: One fabricated 32-bit SFQ string-matching processor achieved up to 251 GOPS/W.
results.detail: The criterion requires 50,000 junctions at 500,000 junctions/cm² and bit-operation performance at 4 K. The abstract does not specify the energy measurement boundary.
results.quote: Our chip has been fabricated and tested, revealing not only its capability for 32-bit bit-parallel processing at a high speed of 12 GHz but also its achievement of an energy efficiency ratio of up to 251 GOPS/W.

results.finding: One fabricated 32-bit SFQ string-matching processor achieved up to 251 GOPS/W.
results.detail: The criterion requires 100,000 junctions at 1,000,000 junctions/cm² and bit-operation performance at 4 K. The abstract does not specify the energy measurement boundary.
results.quote: Our chip has been fabricated and tested, revealing not only its capability for 32-bit bit-parallel processing at a high speed of 12 GHz but also its achievement of an energy efficiency ratio of up to 251 GOPS/W.

results.finding: One fabricated AQFP SR-Loop register-file cell demonstrated 3-bit storage.
results.detail: The prototype occupied 240 µm × 100 µm and used 34 Josephson junctions. The test equipment limited operation to kHz frequencies.
results.quote:
Fig. 2(a) demonstrates the SR-loop writing every possible
3-bit sequence and storing it for two complete passes around the
loop.

results.finding: One simulated AQFP register-file array had a designed capacity of 72 bits.
results.detail: The paper reports hardware testing of the 3-bit cell. Addressed operation of the 72-bit array was verified in simulation.
results.quote:
A schematic diagram
for a 72-bit SR-Loop register ﬁle is shown in Fig. 3.I nt h i s
design, we have a 3 × 3 array of the 8-bit SR-Loop.

results.finding: Across 11 tested AQFP chips, functioning full circuits contained approximately 20,000 Josephson junctions each.
results.detail: The reported 100 kHz is the excitation frequency. One example produced the correct logical AND output after 31 excitation cycles.
results.quote: Fig. 2.  Schematic of 10,000-gate circuits with 20,000 junctions.

results.finding: Functional 1-bit SFQ Josephson memory cells were demonstrated for a proposed cache with <1 ns access time. The cell count is unspecified.
results.quote: Margin enhancement due to quantization, and low operating currents render this cell an attractive basis for a < 1 ns access-time Josephson cache memory designed with a 2.5 µm technology.

results.finding: All 12 FLXTRP1 single-flux-quantum shift-register chips operated with about 108,500 Josephson junctions per chip.
results.detail: The approximately 10 kHz test frequency was used to characterize operating margins and flux trapping. The reported device density uses a smaller area than the full die, which averages about 4.34 × 10⁵ junctions/cm².
results.quote:
Out  of 12 FLXTRP1 
circuits, i.e., twelve 5  mm x 5  mm chips  containing 72 shift 
registers with more than 1.3M JJs, all circuits were found to be 
fully operational.

results.finding: The largest individual RQL shift register on Chip F contained 40,400 Josephson junctions.
results.detail: The density uses both registers and the shared active area. Averaged over the entire die, the density was about 2.9 × 10⁵ junctions/cm².
results.quote:
Test eﬀort was directed to the chips
containing the two largest circuits, with 32,400 and
40,400 Josephson junctions, which together ﬁlled the
3 mm×3 mm active area of the chip.

results.finding: In a 64-cell cryogenic SFQ lookup table, 63 cells operated correctly at 4.2 K.
results.detail: One cell could not be written to ‘1’, even with the SFQ chip tested alone. The supplied journal manuscript does not establish its peer-review status.
results.quote:
We tested the functionality of all 64 memory cells and 
confirmed that 63 memory cells operate d correctly.

results.finding: One single-flux-quantum FFT processor test chip contained 17,455 Josephson junctions.
results.detail: The reported clock rate, word rate, and power do not establish bit-operation throughput or efficiency without a count of bit-operations performed per cycle or per word.
results.quote: The test chip fabricated using a 1.0 $\mu$m 9-layer process consists of 17 455 Nb/AlOx/Nb Josephson junctions (JJs)

results.finding: One 1,024-bit LR-biased SFQ shift-register memory chip operated at 30 GHz across all addresses.
results.detail: The high-speed test shifted data in with 16-pulse bursts and read it out at low speed. The static power estimate does not establish mean access energy.
results.quote:
We
implemented a low-power 1 k-bit SFQ shift-register memory and con ﬁrmed
its 30 GHz operation for all addresses.

results.finding: The seminar abstract reports a demonstration of one 64-bit RSFQ CPU.
results.detail: The abstract gives no capacity for the CMOS SRAM and no accelerator count for the demonstrated system.
results.quote: the talk will then present the demonstration of an 8-bit RSFQ CPU, followed by that of a more complex 64-bit CPU.

definition = "A superconducting classical computer completes the same workload as a CMOS (complementary metal\u2013oxide\u2013semiconductor) computer in the same or less time, to the same numerical tolerance, using less electricity. Both totals include memory, interfaces, power conversion and cooling. Single-flux-quantum logic transmits voltage pulses whose time integral is one magnetic flux quantum. Adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic encodes a bit in the direction of a current. An 8-bit single-flux-quantum processor has operated at 57.2 GHz and 11.2 mW, measured at the processor.". Reason: The definition now explains what the signals encode, identifies a measured processor for comparison and aligns the throughput condition with the completion test.

goal.need = "Data centres used about 485 TWh of electricity worldwide in 2025. In conventional processors, moving data between logic and memory consumes power alongside arithmetic. A supercomputing site at its power limit could run more jobs, including model training, if each job used less electricity. Superconducting switches and wires can reduce both costs, but the savings must cover memory, interfaces and refrigeration. One large-system design requires 395 W of electrical input to remove 1 W of heat at 4.4 K.". Reason: The revised need uses the 2025 electricity estimate and explains the benefit to power-limited sites and the refrigeration cost that determines whether they obtain it.

add statement by Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (S), project 26220904, 2014: "power reduction of high-end computing systems including cryocoolers.". Reason: The Japanese grant documents a refrigeration-inclusive goal for the adiabatic logic approach, which the existing statements do not identify.

edit completion: criterion = "An integrated superconducting computer and an identified contemporary CMOS computer solve the same HPL dense linear system in 64-bit floating-point arithmetic. Report both configurations and the matrix order. Both solutions must pass the HPL scaled-residual check with the threshold set to 16. The superconducting run must finish in equal or less time and use fewer joules. Measure electricity over each full run with both machines at operating temperature, including memory, communication, interfaces, host and control equipment, power conversion and cooling on each side. The result applies to that problem and those configurations."; set_by = "Technology Atlas fallback. No outside body defines the combined comparison. HPL defines the numerical validation test."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; threshold_quote = "A solution is considered numerically correct when this quantity is less than a threshold value of\n16."; threshold_ref = 21; basis = "HPL defines the double-precision problem and scaled residual. The HPC power-measurement methodology provides a precedent for full-run, whole-system measurements. The matched CMOS comparison, elapsed-time condition and strict inequality in total joules are Atlas criteria. C3's notional prototype is one route to an integrated machine."; refs = [6, 21, 7, 3]. Reason: The C3 processor count is a notional design choice, while identical HPL inputs, a common residual threshold and full-run electricity measurements directly test the claimed advantage.
add case "Half-flux-quantum logic". Reason: The IEEE roadmap identifies half-flux-quantum circuits as a distinct digital logic family with demonstrated interfaces to single-flux-quantum circuits.

add milestone after None: "A superconducting 8-bit adder produces correct sums and has its operating power measured.". Reason: The 8-bit adder is a published circuit benchmark with laboratory power measurements in both pulse-based and adiabatic logic before the C3 integration targets.

edit m1: criterion = "Demonstrate a superconducting subcircuit with 10\u2074 Josephson junctions at a density of 10\u2075 junctions/cm\u00b2, throughput of 10\u2079 bit-operations/s and efficiency of 10\u00b9\u2076 bit-operations/J at 4 K. The efficiency refers to energy dissipated at the cold stage."; set_by = "IARPA C3 base-period targets for the SFQ logic track, slide 22."; threshold_quote = "Throughput (bit-op/s) 10 9 5\u00d710 10 10 11"; threshold_ref = 3; refs = [3, 19]. Reason: The base-period criterion now contains only the four programme targets and identifies the source row for throughput.

add milestone after m1: "A 64-bit cryogenic array meets the C3 main-memory or cache targets.". Reason: C3 specified a 64-bit cryogenic array between the single-cell demonstration and the 1,024-bit memory chip.

add milestone after m1: "A superconducting circuit reaches 5 × 10¹⁰ bit-operations/s and 5 × 10¹⁶ bit-operations/J at 4 K.". Reason: The original logic sequence skipped C3's option-period-1 circuit targets between subcircuits and processors.

add milestone after m1: "A cryogenic memory cell stores one bit and meets the C3 targets for main memory or cache.". Reason: C3 defined a single-cell test with role-specific density, access-time and access-energy targets before array integration.

add milestone after m2: "A 16-bit adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron processor operates at 5 GHz.". Reason: The AQFP programme set its own whole-processor target, which distinguishes processor operation from a clock rate measured on an execution unit alone.

split m2 into "A superconducting processor reaches 10¹¹ bit-operations/s and 10¹⁷ bit-operations/J at 4 K." | "A 1,024-bit cryogenic main-memory chip delivers 5 Gbit/s in burst mode." | "A 1,024-bit cryogenic cache chip delivers 30 Gbit/s in burst mode.". Reason: C3 specified independent processor, main-memory and cache results, with different access-time and energy targets for the two memory roles.

edit m3: criterion = "Integrate one 64-bit CPU, two parallel accelerators and 2\u00b2\u2078 bytes (256 MiB) of main memory in a superconducting computer. The C3 prototype targets are a 10 GHz logic clock, throughput of 10\u00b9\u00b3 bit-operations/s, efficiency of 10\u00b9\u2075 bit-operations/J at 4 K and input/output at 10\u2079 bit/s. The efficiency is evaluated at the cold stage, before refrigeration power is counted."; threshold_quote = "Word size (bit) 64"; threshold_ref = 3; refs = [3, 19]. Reason: The integration criterion now states the notional prototype targets without mixing them with estimates for other architectures.
